name: Tendai Moyo
tagline: A Teacher Whose Lessons Outlived the Bell
biography: Tendai Moyo was born in Bulawayo in 1941, the third of six children of a railway worker and a mother who kept a small vegetable garden behind the township house. He grew up in Makokoba, where the streets taught him early that a man's word and his work were the same thing. From boyhood he was the child who read under the paraffin lamp long after the house had gone quiet.

He trained as a teacher in the early 1960s and took his first post at a primary school in Mpopoma, where he taught English and arithmetic for nearly a decade. Former pupils still remember how he stayed after hours to help the slowest readers, and how he bought exercise books from his own pay for children whose homes had none.

In 1966 he married Siphiwe Tshuma, a seamstress from Luveve whose laughter, he used to say, could settle any argument in the house. Together they raised four children — Nqobizitha, Thokozile, Mthulisi and Busani — in a home where shoes were polished on Saturday nights and church on Sunday morning was not a matter for negotiation.

In 1978 he was appointed headmaster of a primary school in Luveve, a position he held with humility for more than twenty years. Colleagues called him the headmaster who swept his own office, because he arrived before the cleaners and left after the last child had gone home. Under his care the school sent hundreds of children on to secondary education.

His faith was the quiet engine of his life. An elder in his Methodist congregation for over three decades, he led the men's fellowship, sang bass in the choir, and kept a small red Bible whose pages were soft from use. When neighbours quarrelled or funerals needed organising, it was Baba Moyo the street sent for first.

Like many Zimbabwean families, his children scattered in search of work. Nqobizitha settled in Leeds, England, and Busani in Johannesburg, while Thokozile and Mthulisi remained in Bulawayo. Every Sunday evening, without fail, he sat by the telephone waiting for the calls from abroad, and he kept every grandchild's photograph in a shoebox he called his treasure chest.

He retired in 2001, but retirement only moved his classroom to the veranda, where he drilled grandchildren in their times tables and told them stories of old Bulawayo. Twelve grandchildren and three great-grandchildren grew up on the rhythm of his voice. In his last years he recorded short voice messages of blessing for each of them, one by one.

In his final years his strength faded gently, and in 2024, surrounded by Siphiwe and their children, he fell asleep in the Lord at the age of eighty-three. He had lived long enough to bury old friends and to bless new babies, and he met his end as he had lived — with a hymn on his lips and no bitterness in his heart.

He leaves behind his wife Siphiwe, four children, twelve grandchildren and three great-grandchildren, and a city full of former pupils who measure their own lives against his example. The family requests that those who remember him honour him simply: teach a child something true, and tell them who taught you.

poem.title: Forever in Our Hearts
lines: You taught us letters on a veranda floor,
And swept your office before the morning light;
A gentle voice that never asked for more
Than honest work and shoes kept polished bright.
Now Bulawayo's streets feel strangely wide,
The choir's deepest note has left the pew,
But every child you taught still walks with pride,
And every prayer we pray still carries you.

name: Sipho Nkosi
tagline: A Harbour Man Who Lifted Everyone Around Him
biography: Sipho Nkosi was born in 1960 in KwaMashu, Durban, the eldest of five children of a cane cutter from the North Coast and a mother whose hymns woke the house before sunrise. As a boy he walked the long road to school barefoot and unbothered, carrying his one exercise book in a plastic bag against the rain. His teachers remembered a tall, laughing child who shared his lunch without being asked.

At nineteen he found work at the Durban harbour, sweeping the sheds before he was trusted with the machines. Over thirty-five years on the docks he rose from general worker to crane operator, lifting containers high above the ships with a steadiness his mates swore by. He never missed a shift in all those years, and he never let a younger man climb where he would not climb himself.

In 1987 he married Busisiwe Mthembu, a nurse's aide from Umlazi, in a wedding the whole street still talks about. They raised three children — Sabelo, Zanele and Ayanda — in a house where the door was never locked to family and the pot on the stove was always bigger than the family needed.

His workmates elected him shop steward, and for fifteen years he carried their grievances to the offices they were afraid to enter. He spoke slowly and listened longer than anyone, and managers learned that when Sipho Nkosi finally stood up to speak, the matter was already as good as settled.

His faith was worn like his overalls — plainly, every day. An elder of his church in Umlazi, he led the men's guild, patched the leaking roof himself, and sat with the families of the dying long after the prayers were done. He said a man who could not sit quietly with another man's grief had not yet learned to pray.

His youngest, Ayanda, settled in England, and the distance pained him more than he ever admitted. He learned the video calls with the patience of a man learning a new machine, and every Sunday after church he held the phone so his grandchildren abroad could see the sea behind him and hear him say, in Zulu, that home was waiting.

He retired in 2020 and took his joy where he had always found it — at the end of a fishing line on the Durban beachfront pier, hat low, thermos at his side. Six grandchildren learned to bait hooks beside him, and every fish, however small, was celebrated like a tournament win.

In the autumn of 2025 he fell ill, and within a short season, surrounded by Busisiwe and their children, he went home to be with the Lord at the age of sixty-five. His last words to his family were a blessing and an instruction: look after your mother, and look after one another.

He leaves his wife Busisiwe, three children, six grandchildren, and a harbour full of men who still tell stories about the steward who listened. The family asks that his memory be honoured in the way he lived — share your lunch, stand up when it matters, and keep the door unlocked.

lines: The cranes still turn above the morning tide,
The pier still holds the place you called your own;
Your steady hands have set their tools aside,
And Durban's heart is heavier than stone.
You listened long and spoke when speech was due,
You shared your lunch and left the door unlocked;
Now every wave that breaks comes carrying you,
And all our days are anchored to your rock.
poem.closing: Rest in peace, Sipho. Your memory is our blessing.

name: Mai Chiweshe
tagline: A Mother Whose Table Fed the Whole Street
biography: Mai Chiweshe was born in 1938 in the Zimuto communal lands outside Masvingo, the first daughter of a farming family that measured its wealth in cattle, rain and children. She learned to plant before she learned to write, and she used to say the soil taught her a patience that no book could ever have given her.

In 1959 she married Takawira Chiweshe, a builder from the neighbouring village, and moved to his homestead, where she bore and raised her children. When four of them grew to adulthood — Sekai, Taurai, Chido and Ropafadzo — she counted herself the richest woman in Zimuto, and she said so often and loudly.

For over forty years she farmed her fields and sold tomatoes, leafy vegetables and her own crochet at Mucheke market. Traders on either side of her stall set their prices by hers, and schoolchildren knew that Mai Chiweshe's stall was where a hungry child could always find a roasted mealie and a scolding delivered with love.

Her hands were never still. In the evenings she sewed school uniforms on a treadle machine by lamplight, mending for widows at no charge and for neighbours at half price. Half the brides of the village walked to their weddings in dresses she had finished the night before, refusing payment beyond a calabash of maize.

Her faith was the foundation under everything she built. A leader in the Ruwadzano women's fellowship, she opened her home for Thursday prayers for thirty years, and her kitchen heard more confessions and consolations than any vestry in Masvingo. She prayed in Shona, sang alto, and believed a hymn could carry a family through any drought.

When her daughter Chido left for England to work as a nurse, Mai Chiweshe wept at the bus rank and then organised the farewell feast. She kept a photograph of every child and grandchild on the wall beside her door, and when visitors asked, she introduced each one — here and abroad — as if presenting royalty.

She buried her husband in 2004 and carried the homestead alone for nearly twenty more years, serving as treasurer of the burial society, arbitrator of disputes, grandmother to eighteen and great-grandmother to nine. In the hard drought years her granary quietly fed households that never spoke of it, because she strictly forbade them to.

In 2023, in her eighty-fifth year, her strength gently ebbed, and she died at home on the homestead with her children around her and hymns at her bedside. She had told them, plainly and without fear, that she was going to see her husband and her Lord, and that they were not to mourn her as people without hope.

She leaves four children, eighteen grandchildren and nine great-grandchildren, spread from Zimuto to London, and a market where her old stall is still called by her name. Her family honours her in the way she taught them: plant in season, feed whoever comes to your gate, and keep singing, even in the drought.

name: Thandiwe Dlamini
tagline: The Midwife Who Welcomed a Generation
biography: Thandiwe Dlamini was born in 1952 in Orlando, Soweto, the middle child of a railway clerk and a mother who took in washing. She grew up in a yard shared by four families, where she learned early that care was not a feeling but a practice — water fetched, wounds cleaned, babies rocked while their mothers worked.

In 1974 she qualified as a nurse at Baragwanath, one of the proudest days her family ever photographed. She chose midwifery and stayed with it for thirty-five years, rising to senior midwife, and colleagues estimated that she welcomed more than two thousand babies into the world — a whole generation of Soweto, delivered by her hands.

In 1976 she married Joseph Dlamini, a school sports administrator with a laugh that could fill a stadium, and together they raised three children — Lindiwe, Sipho and Nomvula — in Orlando East. Their home ran on shift schedules and church rotas, yet Sunday lunch was sacred, and no child ever left that table without being heard.

The babies she delivered came back to her as grown men and women, stopping her at the shops to say, Gogo, you caught me. She kept a ledger of every birth for the first decade of her career, and in her last years she could still open it and tell you the weight, the date and the weather.

Her faith was practical and unshaken. President of her parish women's league for twelve years, she organised the choir's robes, the catering for funerals and the quiet visiting of the sick, and she sang alto with a steadiness the whole row leaned on. Prayer, she liked to say, was simply nursing turned toward heaven.

Her eldest, Lindiwe, settled in Toronto as a pharmacist, and Thandiwe carried the separation with the same discipline she had brought to night shifts. She wrote letters long after letters were old-fashioned, recorded voice notes for her Canadian grandchildren, and prayed for each of them by name every single morning of her widowhood.

Joseph died in 2018, and grief did not retire her — it redirected her. From her garage in Orlando East she began a soup kitchen that fed schoolchildren and the elderly three days a week, funded from her pension and the kindness of neighbours. By 2024 it was serving more than a hundred plates a day.

Early in 2025 she fell ill, and the city she had served turned out to serve her — former patients, midwives she had trained, and children from the soup kitchen queuing at her gate with flowers. She died peacefully that autumn, aged seventy-three, with her children at her side and her ledger of births on the bedside table.

She leaves three children, seven grandchildren, and a mourning city that lit more than two hundred candles in her name. Her family asks that she be remembered not with tears alone but with the instruction she gave every new mother she ever served: hold them close, and do not be afraid.

name: Kuda Mapfumo
tagline: A Quiet Preacher from the Hills of Penhalonga
biography: Kuda Mapfumo was born in 1947 in Penhalonga, north of Mutare, where the Eastern Highlands rise out of the mist like a wall of green. The son of a subsistence farmer and a potter, he grew up between the fields and the timber plantations, and he always said the hills taught him everything he knew about standing firm.

At eighteen he took work on a timber estate in the Honde Valley, and over thirty years he rose from plantation hand to sawmill foreman. The men under him called him Sekuru even in his forties, because he settled disputes before they ever reached the manager's office and never let a worker be sent home hungry.

In 1974 he married Ratidzo Chikore, a teacher at the local primary school, and they built their home together on the family homestead at Penhalonga. They raised three children — Munyaradzi, Nyasha and Farai — in a household where the Bible and the maize field were read with equal care, season after season.

In his fifties he was ordained a lay preacher in his congregation at Dangamvura, and for twenty years he preached in Shona under trees and in tin-roofed halls across the district. He was not a loud preacher; people said he spoke the way the hills look — quietly — and you found yourself believing.

He chaired the district funeral society for many years, that unsung office which carries every family through its worst day. He kept the register, collected the dues, dug where digging was needed, and no burial in his ward ever failed for want of a man to organise it while the family wept.

His eldest, Munyaradzi, settled in Adelaide, Australia, and Kuda bore the distance with a farmer's patience. He learned to send voice recordings across the world, greeting his Australian grandchildren in Shona and English, and he planted a muhacha tree for each of them, so that something in Zimbabwe was always growing in their name.

He retired from the sawmill in 2007 and gave his last working years to the homestead — bee hives on the slope, a vegetable garden he boasted about, and long afternoons teaching Farai's boys to read the weather. Six grandchildren and two great-grandchildren knew his lap as the safest seat in the Eastern Highlands.

In the quiet winter of 2021 he took ill, and within weeks, with Ratidzo holding his hand and the family singing softly at his bedside, he passed on at the age of seventy-four. Because of the restrictions of that season many mourned him from afar, but the hills he had loved received him all the same.

He leaves his wife Ratidzo, three children, six grandchildren and two great-grandchildren, and a district that still quotes his sermons at funerals. The family asks that he be honoured as he lived — plant something that will outlast you, and speak the Word quietly enough that people lean in to hear.

Your quiet Word outlives the passing season,

You planted trees for children far from home,
You read the clouds and taught us how to see;

And every path you walked still leads to Thee.

name: Naledi Mokoena
tagline: A gentle nurse of hands and heart, who carried her church and her family through every storm.
biography: Naledi Mokoena was born on 3 March 1965 in Bethlehem in the Free State, the third of six children of a railway clerk and a seamstress. She grew up in a home where hymns were sung before sunrise and no neighbour's child went hungry, and she carried those two habits — prayer and generosity — with her for the rest of her life.

After matriculating, she trained as a nurse in Bloemfontein and qualified in 1986, the year she moved to Cape Town to take up a post at a community clinic in Gugulethu. The city was far from everything she knew, but Naledi made it home quickly, joining a local congregation within her first month and learning to love the mountain and the sea.

For thirty-seven years she nursed the people of her community through measles and mothers' first babies, through long winters and longer queues. She remembered names, asked after grandmothers, and kept spare sandwiches in her bag for patients who had come to the clinic hungry. Younger nurses called her Mme Naledi and tried to copy the gentleness of her hands.

In 1989 she married Thabiso Mokoena, a high-school mathematics teacher whose quiet humour steadied her through twenty-six years of marriage. Their Cape Town home became famous for Sunday lunches that stretched into the evening, for the pot of morogo always on the stove, and for a door that was never closed to family, neighbours, or strangers in need.

Naledi and Thabiso raised three children — Lerato, Kagiso and Mpho — on night-shift schedules and a teacher's salary, and somehow never missed a parents' evening, a choir concert, or a graduation. She used to say that education was the one inheritance no one could steal, and she lived to see all three of her children walk across university stages.

Her church was her second home. For more than two decades she served in the women's league, eventually as its president, leading prayers, organising winter soup kitchens, and visiting the sick with a basket and a Bible. When a family in the congregation faced a crisis, it was Naledi's number they dialled first, whatever the hour.

When Thabiso passed away in 2015, her grief was deep but never bitter. She spoke of him every day, kept his photograph in a small frame on the kitchen wall, and told her grandchildren that love does not end; it only changes its address. Her faith in those years grew quieter and stronger, like a lamp turned low but never out.

She retired in 2022 to a house full of grandchildren — Neo, Palesa, Katlego and little Rethabile — who knew her lap as the safest place in the world. She recorded prayers and bedtime blessings as voice notes for them, so that, as she put it, they would always be able to find her voice whenever they needed it.

Naledi passed away peacefully on 14 June 2024, aged fifty-nine, with her children beside her and the women of her league singing at the door of her ward. Her memorial service was livestreamed so that family abroad could mourn with those at home. She leaves a legacy measured not in things, but in the thousands of lives her hands touched.
tributesTitle: Tributes from Her Children, Grandchildren and Church Family

scripture.text: I lift up my eyes to the mountains — where does my help come from? My help comes from the Lord, the Maker of heaven and earth.

hymn.original: Ke mohau feela, ke mohau, ke mohau o nthusitseng; ha ke le fokola, Morena, ke wena o ntsitsitseng.
hymn.translation: It is grace, only grace, grace that has helped me; when I grow weak, O Lord, it is You who has lifted me up.

poem.title: Forever in Our Hearts
lines: A lamp is lit beside the mountain tonight,
for the gentlest of nurses has laid down her load.
Her hands that healed a thousand children
rest now, folded soft in the arms of God.
We hear her still in every morning hymn,
in the steam of morogo, in a grandchild's laugh.
She taught us love is a lamp passed on —
and we will carry her light along the path.
poem.closing: Rest in peace, Naledi. Your memory is our blessing.

name: Sekuru Banda
tagline: A keeper of stories and soil, whose wisdom rooted a family across three generations.
biography: Sekuru Banda was born on 12 August 1929 in the communal lands outside Shurugwi, in the heart of the Midlands, the eldest son of a cattle herder and a potter. He grew up herding his father's beasts among the granite kopjes, learning the names of birds, the moods of rain, and the old praise-poems of his people from his own grandfather's lips.

As a young man he left home to work on the railway, laying and mending track across the Midlands for more than thirty years. The work was hard and the pay was small, but he fed a growing family on it, and he never returned home without a gift — a length of cloth for his wife, or sweets wrapped in paper for the children.

In 1953 he married Ruramai, a girl from the neighbouring village whose laugh, he always said, could call the cattle home by itself. Their marriage lasted fifty-seven years, and their homestead became a village within a village: sons and daughters, then grandchildren, then great-grandchildren, all finding their way back to Sekuru's fire.

When independence came in 1980, Sekuru retired from the railway and returned to the land he had never stopped dreaming about. He built his homestead with his own hands, planted maize and groundnuts, and kept a small herd of cattle whose bloodlines he could recite like genealogy. Farming, he said, was not work; it was worship with the hands.

He and Ruramai raised four children — Tendai, Rumbidzai, Farai and Chipo — and sent each one to school even in the leanest years. A full stomach feeds a child for a day, he liked to say, but a full mind feeds him for a lifetime. All four went on to raise families of their own, and the homestead filled with grandchildren every school holiday.

In his later years Sekuru became the elder everyone sought out. He sat on the village dare, settled disputes with patience and proverbs, and was keeper of the family history, able to name seven generations without notes. On quiet evenings he played the mbira, and the young ones learned that a story, well told, could carry a whole people inside it.

His faith was old and deep, rooted in the Methodist mission church where he had been baptised as a young husband. He prayed long prayers at dawn, gave the first of every harvest to the church, and treated strangers as relatives he had not yet met. Even those who argued with him in the dare walked away feeling they had been blessed.

Ruramai's death in 2010 dimmed him for a season, but it did not break him. He took to sitting beneath the big mutondo tree at her grave, talking to her about the rains and the grandchildren, and slowly the light returned to his eyes. She is only in the next room, he told the family, and the door between us is thin.

Sekuru passed away peacefully at home on 2 November 2019, in his ninety-first year, surrounded by children, grandchildren and the lowing of his cattle in the kraal. He was buried beside Ruramai under the mutondo tree, while the village drummed and sang through the night. A great tree has fallen, the elders said, but its seeds are everywhere.

poem.title: Forever in Our Hearts
lines: A great tree has fallen in the Midlands,
and the kopjes stand silent where he walked.
Ninety harvests he gathered with patient hands,
and ninety stories he planted in his people.
The mbira is quiet now beside the fire,
but the song does not die — it changes singers.
Rest, old father, beneath the mutondo's shade;
your grandchildren's children will say your name.
poem.closing: Rest in peace, Sekuru. Your memory is our blessing.

name: Ayanda Khumalo
tagline: A bright and tender light between two homes — London and Zimbabwe — gone too soon, loved beyond measure.
biography: Ayanda Khumalo was born on 17 May 1988 in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe, the middle child of Sipho and Thandiwe Khumalo, in a home where isiNdebele lullabies and church hymns were sung in the same breath. Those who knew her as a little girl remember a child who shared everything — her bread, her jokes, her umbrella — as if kindness were simply her first language.

She grew up between Bulawayo and her grandmother's home in Harare, top of her class and bottom of no one's heart. Teachers wrote 'a gentle leader' on her reports year after year. At sixteen she announced at the dinner table that she would become a nurse, because, she said, sick children needed someone who was not afraid to hold their hand.

In 2008, aged twenty, Ayanda travelled to London to study nursing — the first of her family to cross that ocean. She wept at the airport, then dried her eyes and promised her mother she would make them proud. She kept that promise every single day of the twelve years that followed, though the homesickness never fully left her.

She qualified as a paediatric nurse and worked on a children's ward in north London, where parents came to ask for her by name. Colleagues remember her singing softly to frightened patients in isiNdebele, staying past her shift to sit with worried mothers, and celebrating every small recovery as if it were her own child going home.

London never replaced home; it only joined it. Ayanda's life stretched like a bridge between three cities — her parents in Bulawayo, her sister Nomvula in Harare, her brother Bhekani in Johannesburg. Her payslip had two addresses: rent in London, and school fees, groceries and university costs flowing steadily back to Zimbabwe. She gave quietly and asked for nothing.

At the Zimbabwean fellowship she attended in London, Ayanda found her second family. She sang alto in the choir, organised the winter collection for the homeless, and ran the video calls that kept scattered families laughing together. Friends say she could make a stranger feel like a cousin within five minutes, and like family within ten.

She was the beloved aunt of Zinhle and little Mandla, who knew her face from a phone screen long before they knew it in person, and loved it no less for that. Every parcel she sent home contained something impractical and perfect — a sparkly dress, a toy ambulance — because, she said, childhood should have some glitter in it.

In the spring of 2020, after a brief illness borne with her characteristic grace, Ayanda passed away in London on 26 April 2020, aged just thirty-two. The loss fell on two countries at once. Because travel was impossible in that season, her family mourned across three time zones, gathered around screens, singing the hymns she loved through their tears.

Later that year her ashes were carried home to Zimbabwe, as she had always asked, and laid to rest near Bulawayo among her people. She leaves her parents, her sister, her brother, her niece and nephew, a choir that still keeps her chair, and a ward of children who will never know the name of the nurse whose gentleness helped them heal.

'She was twenty minutes ahead of me in everything and I spent my whole life happily following. Johannesburg feels very far from heaven tonight.' — Bhekani, her brother
'Auntie Ayanda sent me the dress I wore at my first dance. When I miss her, Mum lets me hold her phone and listen to her voice notes.' — Zinhle, her niece

poem.title: Forever in Our Hearts
lines: She flew across the ocean with a promise in her hand,
and built a bridge of kindness from London to her home.
Too soon, too soon, the morning came that called her name,
and two whole nations wept beneath a single sky.
But love like hers does not end at the water's edge —
it travels, as she did, and finds its way back home.
Sleep gently now, sweet nurse, sweet daughter, sweet friend;
your song still lifts the choir; your light still warms the ward.
poem.closing: Rest in peace, Ayanda. Your memory is our blessing.

name: Mbuya Takawira
tagline: A grandmother to many, a gardener of people and of the earth, whose faith held a village together.
biography: Mbuya Takawira was born on 4 April 1935 in the farming country west of Sinoia — the town we now call Chinhoyi — the fourth of eight children. She often said she was raised by two mothers: her own, and the land itself. From childhood she could read the sky for rain and make a meal from almost anything that grew.

In 1956 she married Takawira, a quiet carpenter whose hands, she liked to say, were as honest as his prayers. They built a homestead outside Chinhoyi and raised four children — Mavis, Tapiwa, Ropafadzo and Learnmore — on the produce of a garden that became famous across three villages for its tomatoes, its rape, and its generosity.

For more than forty years she sold her vegetables at the Chinhoyi market, rising before dawn to walk to her stall with a basket on her head and a song on her lips. Other traders watched how she kept her books in a school exercise book, counted every cent, and still gave away the last bundle of greens to any mother with nothing.

Her garden fed more than her own table. Through droughts and hard seasons, Mbuya's dried vegetables — her mufushwa — carried neighbours' families through to the next harvest. She quietly paid school fees for two orphaned girls from her street for six years, and asked them never to say her name aloud. The village said it anyway, with gratitude.

At church she was the treasurer of the Ruwadzano women's fellowship for nearly twenty years, and the women say the money never once went astray, and neither did she. She led the visiting rota to the sick, taught young brides to cook and to forgive, and ended every meeting with the same prayer: that no one under her care would ever feel alone.

Her home was the centre of everything for the whole family. Her grandchildren — Chiedza, Tawanda, Rutendo and little Nyaradzo — grew up shelling groundnuts at her feet in the yard, learning proverbs the way other children learn counting songs. To be scolded by Mbuya, they say now with laughter, was to be loved in the strictest and safest way there is.

When Sekuru Takawira passed in 2008, she mourned him with the dignity of one who had already decided to outlive her grief for the sake of the family. She wore white for a year, kept his carpentry tools oiled and ordered in the shed, and told her grandchildren that a good marriage does not end — it simply becomes a memory you can live inside.

In her last years she slowed, but she never stopped. She directed the garden from a chair under the msasa tree, sang alto in the fellowship choir until her voice grew thin, and blessed every visitor with both hands. When her grandchildren recorded her singing an old hymn on a phone, she laughed and said, 'Now I will never finish dying.'

Mbuya Takawira passed away peacefully at home on 20 September 2018, aged eighty-three, surrounded by her children and with the women's fellowship singing at her window. She was laid to rest beside her husband at the homestead, under the msasa trees she had planted as a young bride. The market closed for a morning in her honour, and the whole town understood why.

name: Pieter van Wyk
tagline: A faithful husband, father and oupa who could fix anything with his hands — and most broken hearts with his kindness.
biography: Pieter van Wyk was born on 9 July 1954 in Pretoria North, the second of five children in a house where the radio played boeremusiek on Saturday mornings and the Bible was read after supper. His father was a fitter and turner, and Pieter inherited both his trade and his temperament: patient, precise, and quietly stubborn about doing a thing properly.

He qualified as a mechanical engineer and gave forty years to the same Pretoria firm, rising from apprentice to the man everyone fetched when a machine 'spoke funny' and no one else could hear it. Colleagues say he never sent a job out that he would not have signed his name to, and that his workshop was the tidiest place in Gauteng.

In 1978 he married Annelie, his high-school sweetheart, in the church where they had both been confirmed. Their marriage lasted forty-four years, and produced three children — Johan, Marike and Christiaan — and a home where the coffee was always on, the garage door always open, and Sunday lunch a law of nature that no one dared break.

Pieter could fix anything: a gearbox, a leaking geyser, a broken fence, and — his family insists — most bad moods. When his father died, he inherited a 1967 bakkie that had stood rusting in a barn, and he spent six years restoring it bolt by bolt. The day it started, neighbours say, he drove it slowly around the block with tears on his cheeks.

His faith was the engine under everything. He served the Dutch Reformed congregation in Wonderboom as deacon and later as ouderling, visited the sick without being asked, and ran a quiet fix-it service for the widows of the congregation — their taps, their gates, their lawnmowers — refusing payment but never refusing a slice of koeksister with his coffee.

As a father he was soft-spoken and utterly reliable, the kind of man who sat through every rugby practice and every eisteddfod without checking his watch. As an oupa to Lian, Anika, Pieter-Jon and little Suné, he was something else entirely: a builder of tree houses, a teller of tall stories, and a soft touch for ice cream before supper.

In retirement he and Annelie moved to a smallholding near Cullinan, where he kept a few fruit trees, an immaculate vegetable patch, and a workshop that became the grandchildren's favourite place on earth. Every school holiday began the same way: Oupa's apron, Oupa's toolbox, and a project that would take exactly as long as the visit.

Late in 2021 Pieter was diagnosed with the illness that would take him. He faced it the way he faced everything — with his jaw set, his humour dry, and Annelie's hand in his. He passed away at home on 28 February 2022, aged sixty-seven, with his children around his bed and the old Afrikaans hymns playing softly in the room.

His funeral filled the church in Wonderboom to the doors, and the men's choir sang 'Nader, my God, tot U' the way he had always sung it — from the chest, slightly ahead of the beat. He leaves Annelie, his three children, four grandchildren, one restored bakkie, and a town full of things he fixed that are still working, like his love.

each in its place, as he would have wanted.
He built his life the way he built his engines —
patient, honest, made to last.
Forty-four years of morning coffee, gently carried,
four grandchildren raised on sawdust and stories.
The old bakkie runs; the congregation sings;
and everything he loved keeps working still.

name: Rudo Chikafu
tagline: Her name was love — and she lived every letter of it, between Harare and Toronto.
biography: Rudo Chikafu was born in the autumn of 1971 in Highfield, Harare, the third of six children. Her parents named her Rudo — love — and family always said the name chose her as much as she chose it. She grew up sharing her schoolbooks with girls who had none, singing in the township choir, and learning from her grandmother that a home is measured by how many people it can feed.

At school, teachers remembered a quiet, attentive girl who asked more questions than she answered. Rudo trained as a nurse in Harare, drawn to work that let her hold frightened hands and explain difficult things gently. On the wards she earned a name for staying past her shift when a patient had no family nearby, and for remembering every patient's name long after they had gone home.

In 1994 she married Tapiwa Chikafu, a quiet engineer with a laugh that filled any room. Their home in Harare soon filled with children — Tendai, Ropafadzo and, later, Munashe — and with the noise of cousins who treated her kitchen as their own. Friends said you could not visit Rudo without being fed, and you could not leave without being prayed for.

In 2001, when hospitals abroad came looking for Zimbabwean nurses, Rudo made the hardest decision of her life. She and Tapiwa chose Toronto, carrying two suitcases, three children and a promise that distance would never dilute their love. She re-qualified as a nurse in a new country, working night shifts through unfamiliar winters, sending school fees and medicine home, and building a bridge between two worlds.

In Toronto she became the centre of a scattered community. New arrivals from Zimbabwe slept their first Canadian nights on her sofa; babies born far from grandmothers were wrapped in blankets she knitted. She sang in a church choir that sounded, on a good Sunday, like a corner of Harare, and she taught a generation of diaspora children the hymns their own grandmothers had sung.

Her family knew her love best through her voice. Every Sunday for twenty-four years, Rudo recorded long voice notes for her mother and sisters in Harare — news, jokes, prayers, and always a song at the end. Hundreds of those recordings survive. In her final months, when travel was no longer possible, the voice notes carried her home; today they carry her family through grief.

In 2019 she became a grandmother, and Gogo Rudo suited her perfectly. She taught her grandchildren Shona lullabies over video calls and snowball rules in the park. Every second summer she flew home, arriving with a suitcase of gifts and leaving with one of maputi and dried matemba — and, always, with tears that finally dried somewhere over the Atlantic.

When illness came in 2023, Rudo met it the way she met everything — with faith, lists, and concern for everyone except herself. She chose her own memorial hymns and apologised to her nurses for being a difficult patient, which she never was. She passed away peacefully at home in the spring of 2025, surrounded by Tapiwa, her children, and the Shona lullabies she loved.

Rudo is survived by her husband Tapiwa; her children Tendai, Ropafadzo and Munashe; three grandchildren; her mother in Harare; and five siblings on two continents. She asked that mourners not weep for her but telephone someone they love instead. Her name was love. In thousands of small kindnesses between Toronto and Harare, that love is still at work.

lines: Your name was Love, and love you gave,
across two homes, across the waves.
In every call, in every song,
you taught our hearts where they belong.
Though oceans keep your resting place,
we feel you near in every grace.
Sleep gently now — your work is done;
two skies keep watch for you as one.
poem.closing: Rest in peace, Rudo. Your memory is our blessing.

name: Baba Solomon Moyo
tagline: He gave a nation its songs, and a township its teacher. The music plays on.
biography: Solomon Moyo was born in 1930 in the Chivi district, the son of a herdsman and a potter, in a world that offered a village boy few stages. He made his first instrument from a paraffin tin and fencing wire, and by twelve he was playing at gatherings across the district. Those who heard the boy play said the sound was already old — as if he had carried it a long way to give it to them.

In the early 1950s he boarded a bus to the capital with his homemade guitar and a change of clothes. He worked by day as a gardener and later a messenger, and by night he played in the township halls of Mbare, where people pressed into the doorways to hear him. It was there that he stopped being Solomon and became, to everyone who loved his music, simply Baba.

In 1956, with three friends from the same township, he formed The Mbare Sunrise Band. Their sound married the rhythms of the village to the harmonies of the church, and it carried. They played weddings, harvest celebrations and Christmas concerts, travelling by bus with instruments tied to the roof. Payment was often a meal and a place to sleep, and Baba always said it was enough.

Through the 1960s the band's recordings found their way onto the radio, and songs like Chiedza — light — became part of the country's vocabulary. Offers came to record and tour abroad; Baba declined them all. His audience, he said, was here, in the halls and the townships and the church pews. Fame never moved him. A full dance floor did.

When independence came in 1980, it was the Sunrise Band that played at the community celebrations in Mbare, and old people still remember dancing that night until sunrise, as the name promised. In the years that followed, Baba's music marked the nation's joys and griefs. His songs were sung at weddings, at funerals, and in long queues, by people who never knew he had written them.

His greatest stage was arguably his own veranda. For more than forty years, Baba gave free music lessons to the children of Mbare — guitar, drums, voice, and, above all, discipline. He fed his students, paid exam fees he could barely afford, and told their mothers, the child will pay me by playing well. Scores of today's musicians, at home and across the diaspora, began on that veranda.

For over thirty years he also served as choirmaster of his church, stopping whole services to teach one child one note. He married his beloved Rutendo in 1958; they raised four children, and after her passing in 2011 he carried his grief the way he carried everything — in song. To his family he was a gentle, funny, stubborn man who fell asleep with a guitar on his chest.

Baba Solomon passed away peacefully in 2022, aged ninety-two, at home in Harare, with his family singing around his bed. News of his death travelled far beyond Zimbabwe; the livestream of his memorial was watched by former students and fans across the diaspora. The tributes spoke of one thing again and again: he gave away everything he had — his music, his time, his love.

This memorial was created and is maintained by the community Baba served — former students, fellow musicians, church members and fans — with the blessing of his family. It is not an official memorial of the estate. It is simply a thank-you, from the thousands who learned a song, danced a first dance, or found a little light, because Baba Solomon Moyo played.

Play on, dear Baba, play on, play on —

name: Grace Nyoni
tagline: She made beauty out of almost nothing, and gave it all away.
biography: Grace Nyoni was born in Kwekwe in 1949, the eldest daughter of a railway worker and a mother who sold vegetables at the township market. From her mother she inherited the two gifts that shaped her life: clever hands and a generous heart. As a girl she sewed her younger siblings' clothes from scraps, and neighbours soon learned that the Nyoni girl could make something beautiful out of almost nothing.

She left school early to help at home, but she never stopped learning. Grace apprenticed with a local seamstress, mastered her trade, and opened a small stall at the Kwekwe market that she kept for forty years. Her sewing machine — bought second-hand and repaired more times than anyone could count — became one of the hardest-working tools in town.

In 1972 she married Jabulani Nyoni, a mine carpenter with gentle manners and a beautiful singing voice. They built a modest home and raised four children — Sipho, Thandiwe, Bongani and Nokuthula — on faith, discipline and laughter. Their house was small, but no visitor ever left it hungry, and no child of the street ever went without a mended shirt.

Grace's stall became a school without a name. Over the years she taught dozens of township girls to sew — charging nothing from those who could not pay — so that they could feed their own families. Many of Kwekwe's dressmakers today trace their trade back to her table. She used to say that a skill given away is not lost; it is multiplied.

When Jabulani passed away in 2010, Grace grieved with the same dignity with which she lived. She sold nothing, moved nowhere, and simply opened her stall the following Monday, because, she said, work is prayer with the hands. Her children begged her to rest; instead she joined the leadership of the church women's fellowship, where widows and young mothers alike found in her a steady anchor.

Her faith was quiet and complete. She arrived at church before the doors opened and left after they closed, and her corner pew became a landmark. When any family in the fellowship buried a loved one, Grace cooked for the whole funeral. When a baby was born, a hand-stitched blanket followed within days. Her hymns, sung in her low, warm voice, steadied many a trembling service.

In her last years, Grace slowed but did not stop. Grandchildren crowded her kitchen for isitshwala and stories; she taught them Ndebele proverbs and the old hymns, and recorded none of it, believing some things should live in memory. Early in 2025, after a short illness borne with characteristic grace, she passed away at home in Kwekwe, surrounded by her children, with her favourite hymn on their lips.

Grace is survived by her four children, eleven grandchildren and two great-grandchildren, and by the dozens of women she taught to sew and to stand on their own feet. Her sewing machine now belongs to her eldest granddaughter, who has promised to keep it working. It is a fitting inheritance: something old, something faithful, still making beauty out of almost nothing.
tributesTitle: Tributes
tributes: Ma sold her sewing machine twice to pay our school fees, and twice she bought another with her savings. She never once called it a sacrifice. She called it love. — Sipho, her son
She taught me to sew and to pray, usually at the same time. Straight seams and a straight heart, she would say. — Thandiwe, her daughter
Gogo made my wedding dress by hand and refused to take a cent. She said a grandmother's stitches are a blessing you wear. — Her granddaughter
Forty years we traded side by side at the market. In hard times she shared her stall and her lunch. Kwekwe has lost one of its kindest traders. — Her market friend
She led our fellowship with a soft voice and a strong faith. When any of us buried a husband, Grace cooked for the whole funeral. — Her women's fellowship sister
She arrived before the doors opened and left after they closed. The church will feel empty without her corner pew. — Her pastor

scripture.text: Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.
For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him.

hymn.original: Woza Moya Oyingcwele, woza, woza; gcwalisa inhliziyo zethu ngokuthanda.
hymn.translation: Come, Holy Spirit, come, come; fill our hearts with love.

poem.title: Forever in Our Hearts
lines: You stitched our days with patient thread,
with quiet words and daily bread.
Your hands made much of little things,
and mended more than cloth and strings.
In every seam a prayer was sewn,
in every meal a love was shown.
Rest now, dear mother, work is done;
your crown is waiting, dearly won.
poem.closing: Rest in peace, Grace. Your memory is our blessing.

name: Farai Gumbo
tagline: He carried lives, not passengers — and brought everyone safely home.
biography: Farai Gumbo was born in Kadoma in 1962, the second son of a cotton farmer, and grew up between the fields and the dusty roads of Mashonaland West. As a boy he was fascinated by anything with an engine, dismantling the family radio and, to his father's alarm, the plough. He left school with a wrench in his hand and a reputation for honesty that never left him.

He apprenticed as a mechanic, but it was driving that claimed his heart. For more than thirty years, Farai drove long-distance buses between Kadoma, Harare and Bulawayo, through rain, dust and darkness. Passengers asked for him by name; mothers sent their children on his bus and slept peacefully. In three decades on some of the country's hardest roads, he never had an accident.

In 1988 he married Chiedza, a teacher at the local primary school, and theirs was a partnership of quiet devotion. They raised three children — Tinashe, Nyasha and Rutendo — in a home where the kettle was always on and the door was never locked to family. He drove thousands of kilometres for strangers, his wife used to say, and saved his best hours for us.

In time Farai bought a kombi, then a second, and built a small transport business run the way he drove — carefully, honestly, and with room for one more passenger who could not quite pay. The young drivers he employed called him Sekuru and learned from him that a driver carries lives, not passengers. Several of them drove at the head of his funeral procession.

His church knew him as its treasurer of many years, a man who counted every cent and accounted for it with pride. The drivers' association knew him as its welfare chairman, who came at midnight when a bus broke down and asked no questions. Kadoma knew him as the man who worked every Christmas so that younger drivers could be home with their children.

Farai's faith was practical. He prayed before every journey, kept a worn Bible in the glovebox, and believed that arriving safely was a promise you kept with God's help and good brakes. At family gatherings he said little and laughed much, happiest with a grandchild on his knee and the smell of sadza on the fire.

In the winter of 2025, after a brief illness that he insisted was nothing to trouble the children about, Farai passed away in Kadoma, aged sixty-three. The news spread from rank to rank the length of the country. Drivers who had learned from him, passengers he had carried safely home, and a church he had served faithfully all came to say goodbye.

Farai is survived by Chiedza, his wife of thirty-seven years; his children Tinashe, Nyasha and Rutendo; and five grandchildren who will grow up on stories of Sekuru's kombi. His family takes comfort in the words he said at the end of every long journey, the engine ticking as it cooled: We have arrived. Give thanks.
tributesTitle: Tributes
tributes: Thirty-seven years of marriage, and he still brought me tea every morning. He drove thousands of kilometres for strangers and saved his best hours for us. — Chiedza, his wife
Baba taught me that a driver carries lives, not passengers. He never had an accident in thirty years on the road. Not one. — Tinashe, his son
He worked every Christmas so younger drivers could be home with their children. We shared him with the whole country, and we were proud to. — Rutendo, his daughter
At every rank from here to Bulawayo they knew Gumbo. If your bus broke down at midnight, Farai came. No questions, no invoices. — A fellow driver
He kept the church's books for fifteen years, down to the last cent. Honest men are rare; we had one, and we knew it. — A church elder
Sekuru let me sit in the driver's seat of his kombi and pretend to drive. He said, one day you will drive further than me. I will, Sekuru. I promise. — His grandson

scripture.text: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.

hymn.original: Jesu ndiye Mufudzi wangu, handizoshayi chinhu; pazororo rake ndinowana rugare.
hymn.translation: Jesus is my Shepherd, I shall not want; in His rest I find peace.

poem.title: Forever in Our Hearts
lines: The long road home, you drove with care,
a steady hand, a whispered prayer.
Through rain and dust, through night and dawn,
you brought us safe — and now you're gone.
The depot's quiet, the road is long,
but in our hearts your laugh is strong.
Park now, dear driver, journey's through;
the road to heaven welcomes you.
poem.closing: Rest in peace, Farai. Your memory is our blessing.

name: Nomsa Dube
tagline: The first hands to hold a generation of Bulawayo.
biography: Nomsa Dube was born in Bulawayo in 1944, in a township where everyone knew everyone and a child's manners were everybody's business. The eldest of five, she helped raise her siblings and decided early that caring for people was not a chore but a calling. She trained as a nurse and midwife at the city's central hospital, the first in her family to wear a uniform.

For over four decades, Nomsa served the mothers of Bulawayo. She delivered babies in hospital wards, in township homes, and once, famously, in the back of a stranded ambulance during a storm. No one kept an exact count, but hundreds of people in that city were first held by her hands. Every child I catch, she used to say, is also mine.

In 1968 she married Mlungisi Dube, a soft-spoken railway clerk who courted her with letters she kept until her dying day. They raised three children — Zanele, Sibusiso and Ayanda — in a home organised with matronly precision and warmed by endless pots of tea. Their marriage of forty-seven years was, their children say, a long conversation that neither wanted to end.

Nomsa's faith anchored everything. She sang in her church choir for forty years, never missing a rehearsal until her knees demanded a chair — whereupon she sang sitting down, louder than anyone standing. In later years she became a church elder, the one who visited the sick, reconciled the quarrelling, and remembered every birthday in the congregation.

Retirement from nursing did not slow her; it merely changed her patients. Every month, from her own modest pension, Nomsa ran a soup kitchen for the elderly of her township, whom she called her schoolmates. She cooked, served, listened and prayed with each one. When donors offered help, she accepted on one condition: that they come and eat with the pensioners, not just feed them.

When Mlungisi passed away in 2015, Nomsa's street rallied around her, though in truth she had always been the one watching over them. She carried her widowhood with open doors and an open table, saying that grief shared is grief halved. Her home remained the place where news was told first — births, weddings, deaths — because Gogo would know what to do.

Her family grew across oceans. A granddaughter settled in London, and at seventy-eight Nomsa learned video calls so she could see her baby's face every Sunday. She recorded Ndebele lullabies for the little one to fall asleep to, and those recordings — Gogo's voice crossing thousands of kilometres — became the family's most treasured inheritance.

In 2025, after a life of eighty-one years and a short illness faced with characteristic calm, Nomsa passed away in Bulawayo, in the city she never left and never wanted to. Her family was at her bedside, and her choir sang outside her window. She told her children at the end what she had told every new mother she ever served: Do not be afraid. Love is stronger.

Nomsa is survived by her children Zanele, Sibusiso and Ayanda; her grandchildren at home and abroad; her two sisters; and a city full of people whose lives began in her hands. The babies she delivered now have grandchildren of their own. It is a lineage of care that stretches, unnamed and uncounted, across Bulawayo — her true and living memorial.

tributes: Ma delivered babies by day and raised the three of us by night. She said every child she caught was also hers. There are hundreds of people in Bulawayo who were first held by her hands. — Zanele, her daughter
She forgave easily and forgot offences completely. I never once heard her speak ill of anyone. That is the standard she leaves us. — Sibusiso, her son

Gogo called every Sunday without fail. When I moved to London she learned video calls at seventy-eight so she could see her baby's face. Her lullaby recording is my most precious possession. — Her granddaughter in London
Forty years in our choir, and she never missed a rehearsal. When her knees gave in, we carried a chair for her, and she sang sitting down, louder than all of us. — Her choir member
Gogo Nomsa fed the pensioners of our township every month from her own small pension. She called us her schoolmates and made each one of us feel like family. — A soup kitchen regular
Our street watched over her after she was widowed, but truly she watched over us. Every funeral, every wedding, every new baby — Gogo was there. — Her neighbour

scripture.text: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth.
And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain.

hymn.original: Uthando lukaNkulunkulu alupheli; lumi njalo phakathi kwethu.
hymn.translation: The love of God never fails; it stands among us forever.

poem.title: Forever in Our Hearts
lines: You caught us first with gentle hands,
the first to hold us, first of friends.
A thousand births, a thousand prayers,
a lifetime spent in others' cares.
The choir will miss your steadfast part,
the kitchen misses your warm heart.
Sleep well, dear Gogo, midwife, friend —
your love in us will never end.
poem.closing: Rest in peace, Nomsa. Your memory is our blessing.

name: Tapiwa Zvobgo
tagline: A faithful farmer, elder and father whose harvest was love.
biography: Tapiwa Zvobgo was born on a clear autumn morning in March 1956, in the Marondera district of what was then Southern Rhodesia. The third of six children, he grew up in a homestead where the cattle were counted at dusk and the granary told the family's fortune. His grandfather taught him to read the sky, and the boy learned early that patience was the farmer's first tool. Those lessons shaped the man he would become.

He walked five kilometres to school each day, often barefoot, carrying his books in a grain sack. After his schooling he found work on the tobacco farms around Marondera, rising from field hand to a trusted position in the curing barns. The work was hard and the seasons unforgiving, but Tapiwa saved carefully, learned everything the land could teach him, and dreamed quietly of a plot he could call his own.

In 1979 he married Rumbidzai, the girl from the neighbouring village whose laugh, he always said, could bring rain. They wed under the msasa trees at her family's homestead and walked home together through the fields. Their marriage lasted forty-six years and was, by every account, a partnership of prayer, hard work and teasing affection. She was his first reader, his last word, and the keeper of every family story.

Independence in 1980 opened a door Tapiwa had been waiting at for years. He acquired a small plot through the resettlement programme and set about it with single-minded joy, growing maize, tobacco and horticultural crops in rotation. Neighbours remember him at the lands before sunrise, hoe over his shoulder, humming a hymn. Within a decade his careful stewardship had turned a bare allocation into one of the most productive smallholdings in the area.

Tapiwa and Rumbidzai raised three children — Farai, Tendai and Chiedza — on a simple rule: school fees before a new tractor. All three finished their education, a fact their father mentioned with more pride than any harvest. He was a firm father but a gentle one, preferring a story to a scolding, and he taught his children that a degree was a crop no drought could ever take away.

His faith was the centre of everything. Tapiwa served for many years as an elder and lay preacher at the local church, opening his home for Wednesday prayer meetings and leading the Sunday singing in his warm, unhurried baritone. The old Shona hymns were his daily companions, sung over the cattle at dawn and over his grandchildren at night. To worship with him, friends said, was to feel that God had simply come closer.

As his reputation grew, so did his service. Tapiwa chaired the local farmers' association and later the community irrigation scheme, where his fairness in sharing water became local legend. He lent seed freely in lean years, quietly paid exam fees for neighbours' children, and settled more disputes with a calabash and a proverb than any court could have managed. Young farmers sought him out, and he never turned one away.

In his later years his family stretched across the world — Farai settled in England, and video calls became the new family fireside. Tapiwa delighted in his grandchildren, Tino and Rudo, teaching them to plant maize in straight lines and to greet their elders properly. Every December the homestead filled again, and he would stand at the gate with his arms wide, counting his blessings as they came up the dusty road.

Tapiwa remained active on his land until his final year, when illness slowed but never dimmed him. He passed away peacefully at home in June 2025, aged sixty-nine, with Rumbidzai's hand in his and his children singing at his bedside. His last words, the family says, were a blessing spoken over each of them by name. The maize was knee-high in his fields that week, green and full of promise.

He leaves behind his beloved wife Rumbidzai, his children Farai, Tendai and Chiedza, his grandchildren Tino and Rudo, three brothers and two sisters, and a community immeasurably richer for his presence. A farmer, an elder, a teacher and a friend, Tapiwa Zvobgo lived the parable he loved most: he was given seed, and he multiplied it — in soil, in children, and in grace.

tributes: Baba, you taught me that a man's word is worth more than his harvest. Everything I grow, I grow because of you. — Farai, son
Daddy walked me to school in the rain and carried my books so they would not get wet. That is who he was — he carried us all. — Chiedza, daughter
Forty-six years we walked together. He prayed for me every morning by name. I do not know how to start a day without that prayer. — Rumbidzai, wife
Gogo says I plant my seeds crooked just like Sekuru did. I hope I grow up crooked like him in all the best ways. — Tino, grandson
He lent me seed in the drought year and refused payment. Pay the Lord, he said. Our whole street is a harvest of his kindness. — Neighbour

poem.title: Forever in Our Hearts
lines: You taught us that a life is like a field,
sown in patience, harvested in grace.
Your hands were brown with honest soil,
your heart was rich beyond all measure.
The msasa trees still mark your seasons,
the cattle know the path you walked.
We plant our grief beside your memory
and reap a harvest of your love.
poem.closing: Rest in peace, Tapiwa. Your memory is our blessing.

name: Lindiwe Ncube
tagline: A gentle nurse and mother whose kindness crossed borders.
biography: Lindiwe Ncube was born in 1968 in Kezi, in Zimbabwe's Matabeleland South, the second daughter of a proud Ndebele family. Raised largely by her grandmother while her mother worked, she grew up fetching water at dawn and singing as she went, a habit that never left her. Those who knew the child said she arrived in the world already caring for people, fussing over younger cousins like a small, determined nurse.

Bright and restless, Lindiwe finished her schooling with the fierce ambition of a girl who had watched too much hardship to accept it. In the early 1990s she crossed the border to South Africa, like so many of her generation, carrying one suitcase and her grandmother's blessing. In Cape Town she found work, studied at night, and in 1993 qualified as a nurse — the proudest day, she always said, of her life.

For more than three decades Lindiwe nursed at a community clinic on the Cape Flats, working night shifts that stretched into years. Colleagues remember her gentle hands and her habit of learning every patient's name by the second visit. To the township she was simply Sisi Lindi — the gentle one. She nursed through epidemics and hard winters, and never once, her colleagues insist, did anyone see her patience fail.

In 1994 she married Bhekani Ncube, a quiet, steady man who had come south from the same district years before. Together they built a modest home in Cape Town and filled it with noise, food and music. Theirs was a marriage of shift-work and sacrifice, of lunches packed at midnight and Sunday afternoons fiercely protected. Bhekani survives her, and the house, the family say, still waits for her key in the door.

Lindiwe raised three children — Nomonde, Ayanda and Siyabonga — with a nurse's discipline and a mother's extravagant tenderness. She sewed school uniforms by hand, checked homework between shifts, and refused ever to let tiredness become an excuse for absence. All three grew into adulthood singing, because their mother sang: while cooking, while cleaning, while praying, and once, famously, all the way through a power cut at Ayanda's birthday party.

She never forgot Kezi. Every month a portion of her wages crossed the border home: school fees for nieces, a sack of mealie meal for her mother, and eventually, brick by brick, a new homestead that she designed over the phone. Every December the family made the long drive north, and every December the old village watched Sisi Lindi arrive like a festival, her boot full of gifts and her arms full of children.

Her faith community was her second family. Lindiwe sang alto in the church choir for over twenty years, led the women's prayer group, and ran a savings club that quietly carried dozens of families through funerals, fees and emergencies. She organised, she cooked, she comforted. When newcomers arrived from Zimbabwe with nothing, it was Lindiwe's door they were sent to, and Lindiwe's table they were fed at.

Grandmotherhood was her final joy. Lwandle and Amahle were raised on her Sunday lunches, her isiNdebele lullabies, and her insistence that children should greet the world politely and then eat properly. She taught them the songs her grandmother had taught her in Kezi, passing a whole century down through one small kitchen. The grandchildren, the family says, are her longest sermon and her sweetest inheritance.

In 2025, after an illness she met with characteristic calm, Lindiwe passed away in Cape Town at the age of fifty-seven, surrounded by her husband and children. Her colleagues formed a guard of honour outside the clinic; patients came with flowers and with stories. In accordance with her deepest wish, she was carried home across the border to Kezi, to rest in the soil that had first sung to her.

Lindiwe leaves her husband Bhekani, her children Nomonde, Ayanda and Siyabonga, her grandchildren Lwandle and Amahle, her sisters in Kezi, and a great scattered family — from Cape Town to Matabeleland — held together by her decades of remittances, recipes and prayers. A nurse, a mother, a chorister and a bridge between two countries, she spent her life carrying others home. At last, home carried her.
tributesTitle: Tributes from Her Children and Family
tributes: Mama worked night shifts and still made our school uniforms by hand. I never once heard her complain. I only ever heard her sing. — Nomonde, daughter
She held strangers' hands for a living and ours for love. Every patient she nursed was family by morning. — Ayanda, daughter
Mum sent money home to Kezi before she bought herself anything. We ate because she sacrificed; our cousins learned because she sacrificed. — Siyabonga, son
Gogo taught me to greet in isiNdebele and to say thank you in every language. I will greet the angels for her. — Lwandle, grandchild
Our choir had many voices, but Lindiwe was the harmony. Altos never get the melody — they make it. So did she. — Choir friend
Patients asked for her by name, even years after she had nursed them. The gentle one, they called her. They were right. — Clinic colleague

scripture.text: Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her. Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all.
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.

hymn.original: Nkosi, wena ukhanya lwami; empilweni yami yonke ngizahlabelela. Ungangishiyi, Somandla; ngiyeza ekhaya kuwe.
hymn.translation: Lord, you are my light; all my life I will sing. Do not leave me, Almighty; I am coming home to you.

poem.title: Forever in Our Hearts
lines: Across the border, across the years,
you carried us in your gentle hands.
A nurse by day, a mother always,
your kindness crossed a thousand miles.
The choir has lost its sweetest alto,
the kitchen misses your Sunday songs.
Cape Town weeps, and Kezi answers:
our Lindiwe has gone home.
poem.closing: Rest in peace, Lindiwe. Your memory is our blessing.

name: Chipo Marufu
tagline: A gift to her family, her market and her choir — a life given away in love.
biography: Chipo Marufu was born in 1951 in the Chegutu district, in a year of failed rains when every family was counting its losses. Her arrival was counted a gain instead, and so they named her Chipo — a gift. She grew up grinding maize before school, drawing water at the river, and laughing, her mother said, more than any child had a right to. The name proved prophetic; she spent her whole life giving.

Formal schooling ended early, as it did for many girls of her generation, but Chipo's education never stopped. She could price a basket of tomatoes in her head faster than any till, and she never forgot a face, a debt or a kindness. Her arithmetic was legendary at the market; her memory for people was better. She used to say that school gives you letters, but life gives you sense.

In 1970 she married Tendai Marufu, a railway worker with a bicycle and serious intentions, and moved with him into Chegutu town. They began with one room and one pot, and Chipo started selling vegetables from a basket carried on her head. Within a few years the basket had become a stall, and the stall had become her second home. Tendai used to joke that he married a wife and acquired an institution.

For more than four decades Chipo traded at the Chegutu market — tomatoes, onions, leafy greens, and the dried matemba fish she was famous for. Her scales were honest, her tomatoes were the reddest, and her credit book was an act of faith: mothers in difficulty were told simply to pay when the rains came. More than one family in Chegutu survived a hard season on Chipo's patience and Chipo's tomatoes.

Chipo and Tendai raised three children — Sekai, Munyaradzi and Nyasha — entirely on the proceeds of that market stall. School fees were paid in small notes counted out at the kitchen table, and no child of hers ever missed a term. She named her youngest Nyasha, grace, and friends say she spent the rest of her life illustrating the word. The children grew up knowing that education was their mother's real stall.

Her second calling was music. Chipo joined the church choir as a young wife and led it for over twenty years, her voice rising above the congregation like a lamp. She sang at weddings, at funerals, at dawn services in the cold, teaching the old Shona hymns to generation after generation. She believed firmly that singing was praying twice, and under her hand forty voices learned to become one.

The women's fellowship was her other pulpit. In her uniform and headwrap she organised, cooked, comforted and fundraised, and she carried the fellowship's burdens as naturally as her market basket. She quietly paid exam fees for orphans, visited the sick with pots of soup, and took in a nephew and two nieces when their own homes broke. Nobody kept count of the people Chipo raised; the whole town simply knew.

Widowhood came in 2010, when Tendai passed away after a short illness. Chipo mourned deeply and then, as her family tells it, stood up, tied her headwrap, and went back to the market the following Monday. Her stall and her choir carried her grief, and she carried everyone else's. In her grandchildren — Anotida and Tanaka among them — she found her last great project, teaching them to sing before they could properly talk.

In her final years the market women gave her the corner stall by the gate, the place of honour, though by then she sold more advice than tomatoes. When illness came in 2025, she faced it as she had faced widowhood and drought: with song. Chipo passed away at home in Chegutu, aged seventy-four, with her children and grandchildren around her bed, singing the hymns she had taught them.

She leaves her children Sekai, Munyaradzi and Nyasha, her grandchildren Anotida, Tanaka and their cousins, her choir, her fellowship, and a market that will never sound quite the same. They named her Gift in a year of hunger, and she spent seventy-four years proving her mother right. Chegutu has buried many of its daughters, but few who fed so many, sang so loudly, or gave so completely.
tributesTitle: Tributes from Her Family and Choir
tributes: Mai, your stall was small but it sent three children to school and fed half the street. You weighed tomatoes and measured out grace. — Sekai, daughter
Mum's ledger was a hymn book. She wrote our debts in pencil and rubbed them out when life was hard. She rubbed out a whole street's debts. — Munyaradzi, son
She named me Nyasha — grace — and then spent seventy-four years showing me what grace looks like in a market apron. — Nyasha, daughter
Gogo could make one mango stretch to feed five children and still save the sweet cheek for the smallest. I was the smallest. I remember. — Anotida, grandson
Forty years we traded side by side. She never once raised her prices in a drought. The market is quieter and poorer without her. — Fellow trader
She taught us that singing is praying twice. When she lifted her hand, forty voices became one. We will keep the song for her. — Choir member

poem.title: Forever in Our Hearts
lines: They named you Gift, and gift you were,
a blessing weighed in open hands.
Your stall was small, your heart was wide,
your ledger written all in love.
The market hums a softer tune,
the choir still sings your harmony.
What you gave away returns to us
a thousandfold in grateful tears.
poem.closing: Rest in peace, Chipo. Your memory is our blessing.

name: Themba Sibanda
tagline: The old guide of the Zambezi whose hope never ran dry.
biography: Themba Sibanda was born in 1940 in a village above the Zambezi, close enough to the great Falls that the spray hung on the horizon like a permanent cloud and the thunder never quite left the air. His people called the Falls Mosi-oa-Tunya — the Smoke That Thunders — and the boy grew up believing, as his father taught him, that the river was a living thing to be respected, read and, when possible, sung to.

His father was a fisherman and tracker, and Themba's classroom was the bush. He learned the moods of hippo, the paths of elephant, and the language of birds long before he learned English. He herded cattle, paddled dugouts, and sat through evenings of elders' stories until the stars wheeled overhead. Everything he later became — guide, teacher, storyteller — was already present in that watchful, hopeful boy beside the river.

They had named him Themba — hope — and in the hard years of his youth the name became his discipline. In the early 1960s he took work as a boat hand and porter at one of the first safari camps near the Falls, carrying bags and listening. He learned his English from visitors, his patience from the river, and his trade from the old trackers. Within a few seasons he was guiding trips of his own.

For over forty years Themba guided on and around the Zambezi — river trips at sunset, walks through the rainforest at the Falls, safaris into the game country beyond. He could read water the way scholars read scripture, and guests remembered not just the elephants and rainbows he showed them but the stories he told while showing them. Through war, change and independence, he kept guiding, and kept hoping, as his name required.

In 1965 he married Ntombizodwa, a teacher's daughter with a laugh he said was worth more than any tip a tourist ever gave him. They built their home in the township near the Falls and raised three children — Zenzele, Sipho and Duduzile — on guide's wages and a mother's fierce discipline. Themba worked the river by day and told its stories at home by night; the children grew up half-wild, well-schooled and deeply loved.

As the decades passed he became the guide other guides consulted. He trained scores of young men from the township in tracking, boatcraft and the old knowledge, insisting that the river's dangers demanded humility before anything else. His evening storytelling gatherings at the homestead became an institution; neighbours' children arrived for the stories and stayed for the proverbs. Many a guide working at the Falls today began on Themba's veranda.

His faith anchored everything. Themba served as a deacon in his church, sang the deep bass line of the Ndebele hymns, and prayed before every river trip, whatever the guests believed. A guide who does not pray, he liked to say, is just a man in a boat. His thanksgiving after safe journeys, his generosity at the church door, and his open home made him as much pastor as guide.

Retirement, when it finally came, suited him. He carved wooden animals for visitors from his chair under the msasa tree, walked with his stick to watch the spray rise over the rainforest, and presided over a growing tribe of grandchildren — Mvelo and Sanelisiwe among the first. With Duduzile settled across the border in Botswana and former clients writing from London and beyond, his veranda became a small parliament of the world's affection.

In 2025, in his eighty-fifth year, Themba passed away peacefully at home, with Ntombizodwa beside him and the distant thunder of the Falls, his family swear, unusually loud that week. Tributes arrived from across the world — from tourists he had guided decades before, from guides he had trained, from a river community that had known him simply as Sekulu, grandfather. The old guide had completed his longest journey.

Themba leaves his beloved wife Ntombizodwa, his children Zenzele, Sipho and Duduzile, his grandchildren Mvelo, Sanelisiwe and their cousins, and a fraternity of guides who carry his knowledge on the water every single day. Named Hope in 1940, he lived up to his name through every season of a changing country. The river runs on, the spray still rises, and those who knew him hear his stories in the thunder.
tributesTitle: Tributes from His Family and Fellow Guides
tributes: Baba knew every bend of the Zambezi and every story it carried. He guided kings and schoolchildren with the same patience. The river will miss its interpreter. — Zenzele, son
My father met danger on the water and hardship on the land, and answered both with the same word: hope. He was named well. — Sipho, son
Daddy sang at my wedding with a voice cracked by age and strong with love. From Botswana I still hear him when the wind comes off the water. — Duduzile, daughter
Sekulu taught me to read the river before I could read a book. Every eddy was a sentence, he said. I am still reading. — Mvelo, grandson
He guided my family in 1989 and wrote to us every Christmas for thirty years. We flew from London for his funeral. That was the kind of man he was. — Former guest
He prayed before every river trip, even with tourists watching. A guide who does not pray, he said, is just a man in a boat. — Fellow deacon

poem.title: Forever in Our Hearts
lines: You were named Hope, and hope you kept
through long dry years and stormy water.
The river knew your steady paddle,
the Falls still wear your morning rainbow.
Elephants pause where you once guided,
the spray rises like a prayer.
Old guide, the journey now is yours —
walk on; the Smoke That Thunders calls.
poem.closing: Rest in peace, Themba. Your memory is our blessing.
